passage: I'm Aditi, and for most of our first year together I thought Ishita didn't love me. When I cried after my grandmother's funeral, she held me but said nothing. When I asked, 'How do you feel about us?', she said, 'Good,' and changed the subject. I took it as coldness. I told my friends she was a wall. Then one night, after another 'good,' she went quiet and said, 'I don't know how to find the words. It's like everything's there, but in a language I can't read.' She'd been making my tea every morning for a year, exactly how I like it. I'd never counted that. Now I ask smaller questions, and I listen to what she does.

qa.q: What had Ishita been doing every morning for a year?
qa.a: Making Aditi's tea exactly how Aditi likes it.

qa.q: Why did Aditi call Ishita a wall?
qa.a: Aditi felt hurt and shut out when Ishita said only "good", and took the missing words as missing love.

qa.q: What did Aditi change after Ishita's explanation, and why might it help?
qa.a: Aditi now asks smaller questions and notices what Ishita does, which lets Ishita show care without needing big words.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ishita to be seen as cold?
qa.a: Ishita probably felt misunderstood and frustrated, caring deeply but unable to find the words for it.

grounding: A young adult looks back on reading a partner's lack of feeling words as coldness, until the partner explains the difficulty.

passage: Counsellor's note, college wellness centre. Hrithik (20, B.Com) came in frustrated about his closest friend, Pankaj; they have shared a room for two years. Hrithik said, 'When his father was in hospital, he never said he was scared. Just "headache" and "can't sleep." When I asked how he felt, he said, "Normal." It's like he doesn't care, or doesn't trust me.' I explained that some people genuinely find it hard to notice and name feelings; it may not be coldness. Hrithik went quiet, then said Pankaj drives him to the station at 5 a.m. every Diwali. Plan: Hrithik will try asking about the body ('headache again?') and offering practical help, and we meet again in two weeks. I've also offered Pankaj an appointment through Hrithik.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say when asked how he felt?
qa.a: Normal.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling on coming to the counsellor?
qa.a: Hrithik felt hurt and shut out, taking Pankaj's lack of words as not caring or not trusting him.

qa.q: Why is asking about the headache a good first step for Hrithik?
qa.a: It meets Pankaj where Pankaj already speaks, through the body, which may open a door more easily than asking about feelings.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel on learning that Hrithik thought he didn't care?
qa.a: Pankaj might feel hurt and confused, having shown care through things like the 5 a.m. station drives every Diwali.

grounding: A counsellor notes a student hurt that his close friend never names feelings, and suggests it may be difficulty with words, not coldness.

passage:
Sunday night
Harsha and I had our monthly 'talk' again. I said, 'I never know what you feel about anything.' Harsha looked at the floor and said, 'I don't know either.' I got angry. It sounded like an excuse. I said something mean about loving a statue.
But then I remembered last week. When I got the internship rejection, Harsha didn't say sorry or anything. Just showed up with my favourite biryani and sat on my floor for three hours doing nothing. And when Harsha's grandfather was sick, the only thing Harsha said was 'my chest hurts all the time.'
Maybe it's not that there's nothing inside. Maybe the words just don't come.
I'll apologise tomorrow for the statue thing.
— Uday

qa.q: What did Harsha bring after Uday's internship rejection?
qa.a: Uday's favourite biryani.

qa.q: Why did Uday get angry at "I don't know either"?
qa.a: Uday felt shut out and took it as an excuse, as if Harsha were cold or hiding something.

qa.q: What does Uday decide at the end, and what might come next?
qa.a: Uday decides to apologise for the statue remark; next, Uday could notice Harsha's actions and body cues as ways Harsha shows feelings.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt being compared to a statue?
qa.a: Harsha may have felt deeply hurt, caring a great deal but unable to find the words, and now blamed for it too.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows hurt at a partner who never names feelings, then a shift toward seeing it as difficulty with words.

passage:
Ganga, 21, texting her boyfriend Tushar after his interview:
Ganga: how did it go??
Tushar: ok
Ganga: just ok? how do u feel
Tushar: idk. tired
Ganga: tushar i've been waiting all day
Tushar: sorry
Ganga: that's not a feeling 😔
Tushar: what do u want me to say
Ganga: anything real. are u nervous? happy? disappointed?
Tushar: i don't know ganga
Ganga: u never know. sometimes i feel like i'm dating a wall
Tushar: ...
Tushar: that's not fair
Ganga: then tell me something
(twenty minutes later)
Tushar: my hands were shaking in the lift after. i don't know what that was. i'm not trying to shut u out
Ganga stared at the message for a long time.

qa.q: What did Tushar say happened to his hands in the lift?
qa.a: His hands were shaking in the lift after.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she wrote that she was dating a wall?
qa.a: She felt hurt and shut out, as if Tushar's short answers meant he did not care enough to share with her.

qa.q: Where is the turning point in this chat, and what could Ganga do next?
qa.a: It comes when Tushar describes his shaking hands; Ganga could ask about that body cue instead of demanding a named feeling, and see that he is trying.

qa.q: How might Tushar be experiencing this chat?
qa.a: He may feel pressured and stuck, knowing something happened inside him but not being able to name it, and hurt that it is taken as coldness.

grounding: It shows a young woman who feels shut out when her partner never names his feelings and takes it as coldness, while his message hints it may be difficulty naming them.

passage:
Sabina had been married to Bhupen for a year when her mother fell ill in the next town. Bhupen shut his tea stall in Nalbari for two days, drove her to the hospital on his scooter, and sat in the corridor all night. He never once said he was worried. When she cried, he handed her a bottle of water.
Back home, she watched him wiping the stall counter, slowly, the same spot again and again.
"Do you feel anything?" she asked. "About Ma, about me? You never say."
Bhupen kept wiping. "I closed the stall."
"That's not what I asked."
He stopped. His ears were red. "I don't know how to say it like you do," he mumbled.
Sabina felt a sharp mix of hurt and something softer. She had heard coldness for a year. She looked at the scooter parked outside, still dusty from the hospital road.

qa.q: How many days did Bhupen shut his tea stall?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling at the end of the scene, and why?
qa.a: She felt hurt and something softer at once; she had taken his silence as coldness, but his red ears and mumbled words made her wonder if he simply couldn't say it.

qa.q: What choice could Sabina make after this conversation?
qa.a: She could look at what Bhupen does, like closing the stall and sitting up all night, and ask him small, simple questions instead of expecting him to talk the way she does.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel when Sabina asks if he feels anything?
qa.a: He may feel ashamed and stuck, because he did care enough to close the stall but cannot find words the way she can.

grounding: It shows a wife who feels her husband never says what he feels and reads it as coldness, while his actions hint it may be difficulty naming feelings.
